text: Writing θ for the class of X in R[X]/(g), the norm of x−θ equals g(x). The reversed linear factor x−X cancels the resultant’s sign, as in [Stoll’s calculation](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L613). Monicity supplies a finite free quotient; irreducibility and separability are unnecessary, and the norm here is a determinant, not an absolute value. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L319), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/AlgebraicGeometry/EllipticCurve/MordellWeil/XSubT.lean#L1080).
For a split monic polynomial, the norm is the product of evaluations with multiplicities.
The elliptic-curve consumer uses the evaluation norm on its nonroot branch.

The norm of the class of p in R[X]/(g) is Res(g,p), with g first. Following [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694), multiplication modulo monic g has that determinant. This is a finite free algebra, not necessarily a field or reduced ring. Even g=1 is covered: the rank-zero quotient has norm 1. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L319), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L332).
The split-polynomial specialization checks product-of-values and multiplicities.
The linear right factor checks the resultant order and sign.

The bounded resultant Res(f,x−X) equals f(x), as in [Stoll’s sign calculation](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L613). Reversing X−x contributes (−1)^m, cancelling the usual right-linear-factor sign. The supplied m may exceed deg(f); keeping this degree bound is intentional. No monicity, invertibility, domain or separability hypothesis is needed. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L332).
The resulting norm of x−θ equals g(x) without a sign.

This spells out [the determinant norm](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/Norm/Defs.lean#L58) on R[X]/(g): multiplication by the class of p becomes q↦pq mod g on polynomials of degree below deg(g). Monicity gives unique representatives and a finite basis, so conjugating by the quotient equivalence preserves the determinant. No field-extension or distinct-root assumption is hidden. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L285).
The Sylvester determinant comparison consumes precisely this conjugacy identity.

Forgetting the inverse of the constructed equivalence leaves the expected Sylvester linear map (u,v)↦gv+u. This matches [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694). The two inputs have degree bounds deg(g) and n respectively; their order determines the matrix convention. Monicity is needed for the inverse, while the displayed equality identifies the actual forward map. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L135), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L141).
The underlying polynomial is gv+u.
The inverse first coordinate is the remainder.

In [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694), the block map sends (u,v) to (pu mod g, v+pu div g). Its matrix is lower triangular, with diagonal blocks multiplication modulo g and the identity. Their determinants multiply, giving the stated equality without a permutation sign. Both degree-bounded modules have explicit finite bases over the coefficient ring. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L285).
The complete norm-resultant comparison uses this block determinant.

This linear map multiplies a polynomial q of degree below deg(g) by p, then takes its remainder modulo monic g. It is multiplication by the class of p on the quotient, expressed using [monic quotient representatives](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/AdjoinRoot.lean#L673). Remainder reduction is essential for closure; polynomial division here needs no coefficient inverses or field hypothesis. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L95), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L271).
The value is exactly the reduced product.
Its determinant equals the quotient-algebra norm.

This is the change of coordinates Ψ⁻¹∘S from [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694), where S(u,v)=gv+pu and Ψ(u,v)=gv+u. Division by monic g identifies the output as (pu mod g,v+pu div g). The supplied bound deg(p)≤n makes the maps land in the indicated finite modules; the block map itself need not be invertible. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L175), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L183).
The first coordinate is the reduced product.
The second coordinate is v plus the quotient.

The equation exposes the defining composition of [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694)’s block map: first apply the Sylvester map for g,p, then invert the one for g,1. Only the latter map is asserted invertible. Monicity and the bound deg(p)≤n ensure the division-with-remainder coordinates are valid over any commutative ring. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L175), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L183).
The composition gives the remainder coordinate.
The composition gives the quotient coordinate.

Monic division gives the unique decomposition q=gv+u with deg(u)<deg(g), as in [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694). If deg(q)<deg(g)+n, then deg(v)<n, producing this linear equivalence. Its inverse uses polynomial quotient and remainder, not rational-function division. For g=1 the remainder module is zero and the quotient coordinate is q. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L141), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L153).
The first inverse coordinate is polynomial remainder.
The second inverse coordinate is polynomial quotient.

Monic division identifies R[X]/(g) with polynomials of degree strictly below deg(g), using the unique remainder as inverse; see [monic quotient representatives](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/AdjoinRoot.lean#L673). This is a linear equivalence, not an assertion that ordinary multiplication preserves the degree-bounded submodule. It requires neither irreducibility nor separability, and g=1 gives the zero module on both sides. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L263), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L251).
The inverse of a quotient class is its monic remainder.
The forward map is the quotient projection.

The equivalence sends a degree-bounded polynomial to its class modulo g, exactly as in [monic quotient representatives](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/AdjoinRoot.lean#L673). Thus it identifies representatives rather than evaluating at a chosen root in an external field. Monicity makes this restriction bijective, even when the quotient contains zero divisors; this does not assert injectivity of the unrestricted quotient projection. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L263).
Taking the inverse of the projected representative returns its remainder.

The first block coordinate is pu mod g: applying S gives gv+pu, and division by monic g removes gv from the remainder. This matches [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694) and explains why v does not appear on the right. Reduction is polynomial remainder, not coefficientwise modular arithmetic, and no invertibility of p is assumed. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L192).
This coordinate identifies the upper-left multiplication block and the zero upper-right block.

The second coordinate is v+(pu div g), since the polynomial quotient of gv+pu by monic g is exactly that sum. This is [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694)’s lower-triangular block formula. The product pu need not have small degree; division supplies the correction. The degree bound on p ensures the resulting coordinate still has degree below n. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L192).
This coordinate gives the identity lower-right block, with the quotient correction below the diagonal.

On forgetting the degree-bound certificate, the value of multiplication modulo monic g is the polynomial remainder of pq. This is the representative formula behind [monic quotient representatives](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/AdjoinRoot.lean#L673): multiplying quotient classes and then selecting the canonical representative. It does not claim ordinary multiplication preserves the degree bound, and polynomial remainder involves no rounding or coefficient division. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L271).
The quotient multiplication conjugacy uses this exact representative formula.

Increasing the right degree bound in a Sylvester resultant multiplies it by a power of the left leading coefficient; see [Mathlib’s bounded resultant law](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Basic.lean#L340). For monic f that factor is 1. The hypothesis supplies a valid upper bound; the natural subtraction used to count extra rows therefore loses no information. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L309), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L136).
The norm formula remains unchanged at every valid right degree bound.
The derivative comparison uses the n−1 bound even when the actual derivative degree drops.

The inverse equivalence recovers the remainder in q=gv+u, hence its first coordinate is q mod g. This is the uniqueness part of monic division in [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694). The degree restriction on u makes this remainder canonical; it is not an arbitrary representative of the congruence class, even over rings with zero divisors. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L175).
The same remainder coordinate computes the first block component for arbitrary p.

The inverse’s second coordinate is the polynomial quotient q div g in the decomposition q=gv+u, matching [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694). Because g is monic, this division works over the coefficient ring without inverting its elements. The degree bound on q ensures the quotient lies below n; no floor division is involved. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L183).
The same quotient coordinate produces the lower block correction for arbitrary p.

The forward coordinate formula is (u,v)↦gv+u, with u the remainder coordinate and v the quotient coordinate, as in [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694). This order matters for the later Sylvester determinant sign. Monicity supplies the inverse, and the respective degree bounds ensure the output has degree strictly below deg(g)+n. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L141), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L153).
The inverse recovers u as the remainder.
The inverse recovers v as the quotient.

By [Cohen §3.3.2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-02945-9)’s root-product formulas, the product discriminant is built multiplicatively from individual discriminants and squared pairwise resultants. Therefore two multiplicative maps agreeing on those inputs agree on it. The target is merely a commutative monoid: neither addition nor cancellation is needed. Positive-degree factors are required; the empty product is handled separately by discr(1)=1. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/MvPolynomial/Discriminant/Basic.lean#L38), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/MvPolynomial/Discriminant/Lazard.lean#L37), [quadratic](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Polynomial/SpecificDegree.lean#L128), [cubic 81](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L125), [cubic −108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L132), [Cubic comparison](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L935). Both concrete Cubic API examples pass: [81](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L164), [−108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L168).
Ambient vanishing orders give a concrete multiplicative-map consumer, including vanishing discriminants.
Lazard valuations provide a second native multiplicative-map specialization.
The native quadratic discriminant formula away from characteristic 2.
The first prescribed cubic has discriminant 81.
The second prescribed cubic has discriminant −108.
The polynomial and Cubic discriminant APIs agree.

The quotient-algebra norm equals Res(g,p) computed with any right degree bound at least deg(p). The extra Sylvester rows contribute powers of the monic leading coefficient 1, so the value agrees with [Stoll’s Sylvester construction](https://github.com/MichaelStollBayreuth/EllipticCurves/blob/66889eada51a74c2f5dfb7fb5909b0b5a0a2d96e/EllipticCurves/Mathlib/Basic.lean#L694)’s actual-degree formula. The bound is essential; no equality is asserted for a degree that is too small. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/AdjoinRoot.lean#L319), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Basic.lean#L77).
The actual-degree norm specialization agrees with the root-evaluation product.
The bounded resultant is explicitly reduced to its actual-degree value.

For positive-degree f and g over a domain, internal root differences give their discriminants and cross differences give Res(f,g)², as in [Cohen §3.3.2](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-02945-9). Leading-coefficient factors balance without monicity. Positive degrees matter: constants have discriminant 1 in Lean, and multiplying by a constant instead follows the separate scaling law. Repeated roots are allowed. Checks pass: [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Product.lean#L94), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L238), [native control](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L287), [quadratic](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/Algebra/Polynomial/SpecificDegree.lean#L128), [cubic 81](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L125), [cubic −108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L132), [Cubic comparison](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RingTheory/Polynomial/Resultant/Discriminant.lean#L935). Both concrete Cubic API examples pass: [81](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L164), [−108](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/FieldTheory/GaloisGroups/Cubic.lean#L168).
The finite-product consequence checks iteration without assuming monicity.

Comparing two converted natural numbers gives exactly their original order. The target may be a partially ordered additive monoid: addition must preserve order, one must be nonnegative, and distinct natural numbers must remain distinct after conversion. No multiplication or total order on all target elements is required. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Order/Basic.lean#L69).

Strict comparison of two converted natural numbers is equivalent to strict comparison before conversion. This uses both order preservation and the hypothesis that distinct natural numbers stay distinct. Only a partial order on the target is needed; the result concerns the ordered sequence of natural-number coefficients, not arbitrary target elements. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Order/Basic.lean#L73).

Every converted natural number is nonnegative when one is nonnegative and adding a fixed element preserves order. The conversion is repeated addition of one, with zero sent to zero. No injectivity or nonzero-one assumption is needed, so the statement also allows different natural numbers to acquire the same value. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Order/Basic.lean#L35).

A converted natural number is strictly positive exactly when the original number is positive, provided one is nonnegative and nonzero and addition preserves order. Zero is therefore excluded on both sides. Unlike full order reflection, this positivity statement does not require all distinct natural numbers to have distinct converted values. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Order/Basic.lean#L53).

The canonical integer map preserves and reflects non-strict order. The target is a partially ordered commutative additive group, addition preserves order, and one is nonnegative and nonzero. Additive inverses let the proof compare the difference of the two integers, so no multiplication or separate characteristic-zero hypothesis is needed. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/Cast.lean#L55).

Strict order between integers is unchanged by their canonical conversion into an ordered additive group with positive one. The group need only be partially ordered, with addition preserving order. In particular, negative integers remain below zero and distinct integer coefficients remain distinct, even though arbitrary target elements may be incomparable. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/Cast.lean#L61).

Converting an integer’s absolute value into a linearly ordered ring gives the absolute value of the converted integer. This is ordinary absolute value on both sides, not a norm or a natural-number remainder. Negative inputs are handled by negation, and zero stays zero under the compatible ring order. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/Cast.lean#L81).

An integer has a nonnegative converted value exactly when the integer itself is nonnegative. This equivalence assumes an order-compatible additive group and positive one. Positive and zero integers are sums of one; negative integers are negatives of positive sums, which cannot become nonnegative under these hypotheses. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/Cast.lean#L49).

An integer converts to a strictly positive value exactly when it is positive. The target needs an order-compatible commutative additive group with positive one, but no multiplication or total order. Thus the comparison with zero is faithfully preserved for positive, zero and negative integers under the stated hypotheses. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/Cast.lean#L65).

Converting the larger of two natural numbers gives the larger of their converted values. The target is a linearly ordered semiring whose order is compatible with its arithmetic. This follows by preserving the comparison between the two inputs, including equality; it does not introduce any subtraction or division. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Order/Ring.lean#L45).

Converting the smaller of two natural numbers gives the smaller of their converted values in a linearly ordered semiring with compatible arithmetic. Both sides select the same input because conversion preserves its comparison with the other input. Equal inputs and zero are included, with no rounding or subtraction involved. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Cast/Order/Ring.lean#L40).

Converting the maximum of two integers into a linearly ordered ring gives the maximum of their converted values. Order preservation selects the same input on both sides, whether the integers are positive, negative or equal. The statement uses the ring’s order, with its required compatibility with addition and multiplication. Compared with [Aspnes §§4.2,4.6](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Algebra/Order/Ring/Cast.lean#L78).

For a finite family of finite types, the size of their tagged disjoint union is the sum of their sizes. An element records both its index and its value, so equal values at different indices count separately. Empty component types contribute zero, and an empty index type gives an empty union. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.3](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L234).

An injection into a finite type cannot increase the number of elements: the source has at most the target’s size. Only the target is assumed finite; injectivity then forces the source to be finite too. This hypothesis avoids misleading comparisons caused by the convention assigning zero to infinite natural-valued cardinalities. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L92).

A surjection from a finite type reaches at most as many distinct elements as the source contains. Only the source is assumed finite; surjectivity makes the target finite as well. Empty cases are included. The finite-source condition matters because the natural-valued count assigns zero to infinite types. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L96).

A map into a finite type is bijective exactly when it is injective and the two types have equal sizes. Injectivity makes the source finite; equal size then leaves no target element missing. The finite-target hypothesis is essential: an injective shift of the natural numbers has equal zero-counts but is not surjective. Compared with [Aspnes §§11.1.1–11.1.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L104).

A map from a finite type is bijective exactly when it is surjective and source and target have equal sizes. Surjectivity makes the target finite, and equal size rules out collisions. The source finiteness hypothesis is necessary; equality of the default zero-counts for infinite types would not rule out a many-to-one surjection. Compared with [Aspnes §§11.1.1–11.1.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L114).

A type has natural-valued cardinality one exactly when there is an element equal to every element of the type. The existence clause excludes the empty type; the equality clause excludes any second element. No separate finiteness hypothesis is needed, since a positive count already rules out the infinite zero-count convention. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L202).

After fixing an element x, the type has cardinality two exactly when there is exactly one element different from x. The uniqueness quantifier is restricted to elements unequal to x, so it supplies one additional element and excludes any third. Infinite types cannot satisfy the condition, despite their default zero-count. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L209).

A type has cardinality two exactly when two distinct elements together exhaust it. The distinctness condition prevents counting one element twice, and the exhaustion condition excludes additional elements. No finite-type assumption is required: either side itself forces finiteness, so the zero value assigned to infinite types causes no ambiguity. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L206).

If a function is injective on a set, its image has the same natural-valued cardinality as that set. Injectivity outside the set is unnecessary. Finite sets retain their ordinary size; an infinite set has an infinite image, so both sides take the designated zero value in that case. Compared with [Aspnes §§11.1.1,3.5.5](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L152).

An injective function has a range with the same natural-valued cardinality as its domain: restricting the codomain to actual outputs makes it a bijection. The surrounding codomain may contain other elements and need not be finite. Infinite domains and ranges both receive the default count zero. Compared with [Aspnes §§11.1.1,3.5.5](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/SetTheory/Cardinal/Finite.lean#L177).

The closed integer interval from a to b contains max(b+1−a,0) integers. Both endpoints count when a≤b, so a=b gives one element. The subtraction happens in the integers, then conversion to a natural number replaces negative results by zero; reversed intervals are therefore counted as empty. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Int/Interval.lean#L96).

The closed natural-number interval from a to b has b+1−a elements, with natural subtraction truncated at zero. Thus equal endpoints give one element and reversed endpoints give none. The addition of one occurs before subtraction; replacing the expression by (b−a)+1 would incorrectly count reversed intervals as nonempty. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Order/Interval/Finset/Nat.lean#L83).

The natural-number interval including a and excluding b has b−a elements, using subtraction truncated at zero. When a<b this is the usual interval length; when a=b or a>b the interval is empty. The excluded upper endpoint is why no extra one appears in this formula. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Order/Interval/Finset/Nat.lean#L84).

There are b+1 natural numbers at most b: the interval consists of 0,1,…,b, including both zero and the upper endpoint. In particular the count at b=0 is one, not zero. This relies on the ambient numbers being natural; the corresponding integer lower-unbounded interval would be infinite. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Order/Interval/Finset/Nat.lean#L93).

The divisors of m*n are exactly all products of a divisor of m and a divisor of n. These form a set, so repeated products are counted only once; coprimality is not required. If either input is zero, its chosen divisor set is empty, and the formula still agrees on both sides. Compared with [Aspnes §8.3](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Finset/NatDivisors.lean#L25).

For coprime m and n, multiplying a divisor of m by a divisor of n determines the two factors uniquely. Coprimality prevents prime factors from moving between the two sides. If either number is zero, the relevant finite divisor set is empty, so the restricted injectivity assertion holds vacuously. Compared with [Aspnes §8.3](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Finset/NatDivisors.lean#L52).

The cyclic subgroup generated by an element has size equal to its order. For finite order this counts the distinct powers before repetition. For infinite order, both the natural-valued cardinality and the order function use zero by convention; the subgroup is still infinite, not empty. The ambient group need not be commutative. Compared with [Judson §4.1](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/ZMod/QuotientGroup.lean#L160).

The subgroup of all integer multiples of an element has natural-valued cardinality equal to its additive order. A finite order is the least positive multiple giving zero. Infinite additive order is encoded by zero, matching the zero-count assigned to an infinite subgroup; the zero element itself generates a singleton of size one. Compared with [Judson §4.1](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/ZMod/QuotientGroup.lean#L160).

A finite type with n elements has n! permutations, where a permutation means a bijection from the type to itself. The formula needs no chosen ordering of the elements. For the empty type there is one empty bijection, agreeing with 0!=1; the explicit finiteness assumption excludes the infinite zero-count convention. Compared with [Aspnes §11.1.5.1](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Finite/Perm.lean#L37).

Coprime natural numbers remain coprime after conversion into any commutative ring. Here ring coprimality means that some linear combination of the two converted elements equals one. Integer Bézout coefficients provide that combination, even in positive characteristic. This is a forward implication; conversion need not preserve noncoprimality or be injective. Compared with [Judson Cor.2.2.3, §16.3](https://judsonbooks.org/aata-files/aata-20260811.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/RingTheory/Coprime/Lemmas.lean#L55).

After conversion into a characteristic-zero division semiring, choosing a objects from a+b equals (a+b)! divided by a!*b!. The division is in the target algebra, not rounded natural division. Characteristic zero keeps both factorials nonzero, including a=0 or b=0 where 0!=1, so no division-by-zero convention is used. Compared with [Aspnes §11.2](https://www.cs.yale.edu/homes/aspnes/classes/202/notes-2013.pdf) and the [pinned source](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/Data/Nat/Choose/Cast.lean#L37).

A class function is precisely a function constant under g ↦ hgh⁻¹. The carrier imposes that equality for every pair of group elements, and pointwise addition and scalar multiplication preserve it. This realizes the usual class-function space over any semiring; neither a finite group nor a topology is assumed. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L52).
A function is a class function exactly when it is invariant under conjugation.

This packages g ↦ tr(ρ(g)) as a conjugacy-invariant function: conjugate group elements act by conjugate linear maps. Finite-dimensional representations give the usual character. The declaration also allows infinite-dimensional spaces, where Mathlib defines trace to be zero when no finite basis exists; that extension remains conjugacy invariant. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L298); [trace convention](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Trace.lean#L75).
The class function of a representation evaluates to its character.

This sends a class function f to the function [g] ↦ f(g) on conjugacy classes. The equality of values on conjugate elements makes evaluation independent of the representative. The construction descends through the quotient itself, so it introduces no distinguished representative and requires no finiteness assumption. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L79).
Evaluating the induced function on the class of `g` gives the value at `g`.

Membership means exactly f(hgh⁻¹) = f(g) for all g and h. The right side is the defining carrier condition, with the conjugating element in the correct order. It applies to arbitrary group elements and semiring-valued functions; there is no additional character, continuity or finite-group condition hidden in membership. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L63).

A bundled finite-dimensional representation gives the class function g ↦ tr(ρ(g)). Its bundle already supplies finite dimensionality, so the trace is the ordinary matrix trace, independent of basis. Conjugation invariance follows from invariance of trace under similarity. The group itself need not be finite for this construction. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L317).
The class function of a bundled finite-dimensional representation evaluates to its character.

The class function of a bundled finite-dimensional representation is the class function of the
underlying representation: `FDRep.character` is `Representation.character` of `V.ρ`.

Evaluating the packaged class function at g returns exactly the original representation character tr(ρ(g)); no averaging or normalization is introduced. Finite dimensionality is absent from this statement: on an infinite-dimensional vector space the underlying Mathlib trace is defined as zero, so the same evaluation identity still holds. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L303); [trace convention](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/2cabef97b63d3275776b8b060d802de6a6fa1055/Mathlib/LinearAlgebra/Trace.lean#L75).

Evaluation of the class function attached to a finite-dimensional representation is its character value at g. Both sides use the trace of the same representing linear map. Finite dimensionality is already part of the representation bundle, and the equality does not require the group to be finite. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L321).

Evaluating the descended function on the conjugacy class containing g gives f(g). This is the defining evaluation rule for quotient descent, justified by the class function having equal values at all representatives. The result is independent of any ordering of the conjugacy classes and holds for infinite groups too. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L83).

For a group homomorphism φ : H → G, this sends f to f ∘ φ. Homomorphisms carry conjugates to conjugates, so the composite is a class function on H. Pointwise addition and scalar multiplication make the operation linear. Subgroup restriction is included, and φ need not be injective. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L118).
A pulled-back class function is the composite with the homomorphism.
Pulling back along the identity homomorphism changes nothing.

Pullback is contravariantly functorial: pulling back along a composite is pulling back along
each factor in turn.

The pullback along φ : H → G evaluates at x ∈ H as f(φ(x)). This is ordinary precomposition, with the direction from class functions on G to those on H. The homomorphism preserves conjugation, which is exactly what ensures the resulting function still satisfies the class-function condition. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L128).

Conjugate elements g and h have the same value under a class function. The conjugacy hypothesis supplies h = xgx⁻¹, and the defining invariance gives the displayed equality after reversing its sides. This is the representative-independence needed for functions on conjugacy classes, over arbitrary semiring coefficients. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L73).

The class function of a bundled finite-dimensional representation equals the class function obtained from its underlying representation. Both constructions evaluate to the trace of the same action at every group element. This confirms compatibility between the two interfaces; forgetting the bundle does not change the space, action or character. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L326).

For a finite group, partitioning the sum by conjugacy classes gives ∑C |C|f(C). Here C.carrier contains the actual elements of C, so Nat.card is its finite size. That integer is cast into the coefficient semiring, allowing positive characteristic. There is no division by the group order in this formula. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L260).

This is the indicator of the conjugacy class containing x: it takes value one at conjugates of x and zero elsewhere. It is obtained by pulling back the singleton indicator on the quotient of conjugacy classes. Thus it is constant on each class without assuming that the group is finite. Compared with [Etingof §4.2](https://math.mit.edu/~etingof/cltrunc.pdf#page=23) and [source](https://github.com/TauCetiProject/TauCeti/blob/b257e0ff255355b2b692c1311d061d2b4dc84e53/TauCeti/RepresentationTheory/CharacterTable/ClassFunction.lean#L244).
The defining values of `TauCeti.ClassFunction.classIndicator`.

At y, the conditional returns one if [y] = [x] and zero otherwise. Equality of these classes means conjugacy. The decision procedure determines which branch applies, without changing its value. Since the coefficient semiring may have 1 = 0, the output need not distinguish membership in the conjugacy class.
